guide.title: Personal Color Guide
guide.intro: If personal color is new to you, the terms can feel a little confusing. This guide walks you through what personal color is, how warm and cool tones differ, what each of the 12 types feels like, and how to put your result to work in everyday life. Take your time, and try holding colors up to your own face as you read.

sections.title: What is personal color?
paragraphs: Personal color is the range of colors that blend naturally with the tones in a person's skin, hair, and eyes. You may have noticed that the same red lipstick can make one person's face glow while on someone else it seems to sit apart from the face. That difference comes from how well the color matches your own coloring.

When a flattering color sits near your face, skin can look clearer, features can look more defined, and your overall look feels fresh. A color that clashes can make your complexion look dull or tired. Knowing your personal color helps you choose makeup, clothes, hair color, and accessories with less trial and error, and fewer disappointing purchases.
Still, personal color is a guide for finding what suits you better, not a strict rule. If a color you love is outside your type, you do not have to give it up. There are other ways to wear it.

sections.title: How to tell warm from cool
paragraphs: Warm tones carry a yellow, golden undertone, while cool tones carry a blue, pinkish undertone. The methods below are easy things to try at home, but they are only rough hints. Rather than trusting any single one, look at several together.
items: Check the veins on your inner wrist: In natural light, veins that look greenish may point to warm, and veins that look blue or purple may point to cool. If you see both, you may be somewhere in between.
Try gold and silver jewelry: If gold blends in with your skin, you may lean warm. If silver looks cleaner on you, you may lean cool.

Compare white and ivory fabric: Hold a pure white cloth and a yellowish ivory cloth under your face in turn. If your face looks clearer against white, you may lean cool. If ivory feels more comfortable, you may lean warm.

Think about how your skin reacts to the sun: People who tend to turn red and rarely tan are often cool, while those who tan to a golden bronze are often warm. This varies a lot from person to person, so treat it as a loose reference.
Look at your hair and eye color: Brown or amber shades sometimes go with warm, while very dark or bluish-black shades sometimes go with cool. Again, this is only a tendency.

sections.title: Reading tone through lightness and saturation
paragraphs: Warm and cool alone cannot describe all 12 types, so we also look at lightness (how light or dark a color is) and saturation (how vivid or muted it is).

High lightness is called Light and low lightness is called Deep. Light colors feel airy and soft, as if mixed with white, while deep colors feel dark and weighty. High saturation is called Bright and low saturation is called Mute. Bright colors are clear and vivid and catch the eye, while muted colors have a touch of gray and feel calm and subtle.

Take pink as an example. A pale, airy pink leans Light, a clear and vivid pink leans Bright, and a dusty, quiet pink leans Mute. Adding lightness and saturation to warm and cool lets you narrow down your colors much more precisely.

sections.title: The four seasons
paragraphs: Litmus Face uses 12 types: each of the four seasons is split into three tones. The season names are simply a handy way to picture the overall mood of a group of colors.
items: Spring: A warm, radiant mood. Fresh, lively colors suit it well. It includes Bright Spring, True Spring, and Light Spring.
Summer: A cool, soft mood. Gentle colors with a blue undertone suit it well. It includes True Summer, Soft Summer, and Light Summer.
Autumn: A calm, deep mood. Warm colors like soil and fallen leaves suit it well. It includes True Autumn, Soft Autumn, and Dark Autumn.
Winter: A crisp, urban mood. Cool colors with strong contrast suit it well. It includes True Winter, Dark Winter, and Bright Winter.

sections.title: The 12 types at a glance
paragraphs: Here is a one-line feel for each type. Tap a type to see its full palette, best colors, and styling tips.
items: True Spring: Warm, playful colors with a yellow undertone.
Bright Spring: Clear, vivid warm colors for a lively look.
Light Spring: Light, pastel-like warm colors.
True Summer: Clean, cool colors with a blue undertone.
Soft Summer: Calm, elegant colors with a hint of gray.
Light Summer: Bright, gentle, cool pastels.
True Autumn: Rich, warm colors with golden and brown notes.
Soft Autumn: Cozy, low-saturation earthy tones.
Dark Autumn: Deep, rich warm colors with a mature feel.
True Winter: Cold, crisp colors with a strong blue undertone.
Dark Winter: Dark, intense colors with strong contrast.
Bright Winter: Vivid, striking colors with sharp contrast.

sections.title: Getting a more accurate self-test
paragraphs: Self-test results can shift easily with your surroundings. Following the points below makes your comparisons much more reliable.
items: Lighting: Check in natural light by a window during the day if you can. Yellow bulbs and fluorescent lights change how skin looks.
Makeup: Go bare-faced or with very light makeup. Heavy foundation or color can hide your natural skin tone.
Screen settings: Turn off night mode and blue-light filters, and raise the brightness. Devices show color a little differently, so compare on the same screen.
Compare side by side: Do not judge one color alone. Try several in a row and see which makes your face look clearest. Differences stand out more the more you compare.
Ask someone else: You are so used to your own face that subtle changes are easy to miss. Ask a friend or family member which looks better.
Try more than once: Test at different times and in different lighting, and focus on the result that keeps coming up.

sections.title: Putting your personal color to use
paragraphs: Once you know your type, apply it one step at a time. You do not need to change everything at once. Starting with what sits close to your face usually makes the biggest difference.
Colors far from your face, such as pants, shoes, and bags, are less affected by personal color. Feel free to enjoy your favorite colors there.
items: Makeup: Start with colors that touch your face directly, like lip, blush, and eyeshadow. It can also help when choosing a foundation shade.

Clothing: What matters most is the color near your face, such as tops, scarves, and collars. Keep flattering colors close to your face, and use a favorite but less suitable color on the bottom half or in small pieces.
Hair color: If you are thinking about dyeing, a shade in the same family as your tone often looks natural and brightens the skin. Talk it over thoroughly with a professional beforehand.
Accessories: The metal and gem colors of earrings and necklaces near your face also matter. Warm types often suit gold, and cool types often suit silver.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions
items:
Q. Does personal color change?
A. It is based on your natural skin, hair, and eye color, so the big picture rarely changes. A heavy tan or a change in skin condition may make it look different for a while.

Q. Should I avoid colors outside my type?
A. Not at all. Personal color is a reference for finding what suits you better. You can still enjoy other colors on the bottom half or as small accents, or place a flattering color between them and your face.

Q. How accurate is a photo-based self-test?
A. It can vary with lighting, camera, and screen settings, so it is best used as a reference. Running it several times and checking with real colors in front of a mirror helps even more.

Q. I really cannot tell if I am warm or cool.
A. Many people sit somewhere in between. In that case, do not insist on one side. Start with soft colors where the two families overlap and see which feels most comfortable.
